quote: Wie für irrationale $x$? Dabei bedeutet $(x) = x-[x]$, wo $[x]$ die größte in $x$ enthaltene ganze Zahl ist.
english: What about irrational x? Here (x) = x - [x], where [x] is the greatest integer contained in x.
topic: A list of research topics: the limit of averages of fractional parts (x), a direct proof of the Dedekind–Riemann reciprocity law via Gauss's method, elementary divisors of linear substitutions preserving quadric or cubic surfaces, semiconvergent expansion of zeros of spherical functions (cf. Stokes), and expansion of integrals.

triage.modern_statement: This is most likely about the average of the fractional parts {kx} = kx − ⌊kx⌋. For rational x = p/q, the average (1/n)·Σ_{k=1}^{n} {kx} can be computed directly: it tends to (q−1)/(2q). The question asks what lim_{n→∞} (1/n)·Σ_{k=1}^{n} {kx} is when x is irrational, and more generally how the values {kx} are distributed in [0,1). In modern terms the answer is: if x is irrational, the sequence {kx} is equidistributed mod 1. So for every Riemann-integrable f on [0,1], (1/n)·Σ f({kx}) tends to ∫_0^1 f(t) dt. With f(t) = t, the limit is 1/2. This reading is an inference from the page topic, since the note itself is only one line.
triage.answered_by: Piers Bohl, Wacław Sierpiński and Hermann Weyl proved it independently in 1909–1910 (the equidistribution theorem). Weyl's 1916 paper 'Über die Gleichverteilung von Zahlen mod. Eins' (Math. Ann. 77) added the general Weyl criterion. That the limit of the averages is 1/2 follows immediately from equidistribution.

evidence.claim: The equidistribution theorem says that the sequence a, 2a, 3a, … mod 1 is uniformly distributed for irrational a. Weyl, Sierpiński and Bohl proved it separately in 1909 and 1910, and variants are still studied today.
The result on irrational rotation sequences was the first equidistribution-type result, proved independently by Bohl, Sierpiński and Weyl around 1910.
Weyl's equidistribution theorem (1909) concerns the fractional parts {a} of integer multiples of an irrational number. Its proof uses Weyl's criterion based on exponential sums.

triage.why: Hilbert's note is a single line asking what happens for irrational x, with (x) defined as the fractional part. The page topic says the item is about the limit of averages of (x). The natural reading is the limit of (1/n)·Σ (kx). For irrational x that limit is 1/2, and the result was settled by the Bohl–Sierpiński–Weyl equidistribution theorem of 1909–1910. It is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Equidistribution and discrepancy theory are still active research areas, and the Wikipedia article notes that variants are still studied. Confidence is medium rather than high because the note is short. It might instead refer to a different average (for example (1/n)·Σ (x/k), or the finer behaviour of the error Σ({kx} − 1/2), studied later by Hardy–Littlewood and Ostrowski around 1922). My sources only cover the equidistribution result.
